scenario: A coffee buyer has been choosing by store rating and is now comparing four frozen offers: a near-perfect-rated whole-bean blend, a highly rated ground-coffee six-pack, a highly rated whole-bean offer marketed as fresh roasted, and near-perfect-rated single-serve pods whose seller says the design preserves aroma and flavor. Community discussions recommend fresh local beans, mention grocery-shelf turnover and bulk subscriptions, and disagree implicitly about how long a large purchase remains good. The research set also contains background on roast chemistry, coffee compounds, bags, barriers, and other sensory quality dimensions. It does not contain a verified roast or pack date, exact lot age, seal or oxygen test, warehouse history, matched review sample, or controlled tasting for any exact offer.
target: Decide whether coffee freshness is a real quality axis without treating it as the only axis or using ratings, seller adjectives, package format, valves, or community impressions as proof about an exact lot. Explain what roast chemistry and typical staling evidence can and cannot establish; audit each exact offer's date, lot, package, storage, form, consumption fit, protections, and true consumed cost; preserve the scope of community statements; control other coffee and brewing variables; and end with a small reversible tasting rule that chooses only the cheapest exact coffee passing every gate, buys a dated fresh reference for calibration, or defers.
